ESSAY | Creating a Distinct Blend of Voices to Tell a Difficult Story

Rushford author’s new suite of poetry and narrative storytelling tell the difficult story of illness, survival and a life-saving heart transplant

By Tom Driscoll, August 18, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
0:00 / 8:32
Instaread

Well-told, timely stories bring people together—we’re glad you’re with us! As a nonprofit we depend on your support to keep this magazine accessible to everyone.

Together, we can do this.

Donate now(opens in new tab)

In 2011, Tom Driscoll founded Winona-based Shipwreckt Books Publishing Company and went to work helping others share their stories. Five years later, unforeseen events caused him to reflect on telling his own story, the results of which make up his extraordinary “non-linear narrative” compilation, “Dying Man Suite.”

RUSHFORD & WINONA—It’s been a couple months since Rocket Science Press published “Dying Man Suite”—just long enough to give me time to think about how I want to summarize my hybrid poetry collection, wandering narrative memoir, and precision timeline of Dying Man logged in hospital clinical notes. 

The esteemed poet Ken McCullough, my primary editor, told an audience at Rochester’s Chateau Theater rollout in June, “This is a difficult book.” 

No argument from the author. 

Author Tom Driscoll, at right, and guests at the launch of his book, “Dying Man Suite.” From left, poet and Registered Nurse Ariel Boswell, a writer-at-the-bedside with the Dolores Jean Lavins Center for the Humanities at Mayo Clinic; book editor Ken McCullough, former Winona Poet Laureate (standing in the back); and Jean Prokott, Rochester Poet Laureate. (Submitted photo)

But I did not set out to create a difficult book; I set out to tell a difficult personal story.

The biggest obstacle to that tale’s accessibility, I think, lies in the book’s hybrid nature, the “Suite” of songs, voices, and points of view, which make approaching one individual’s descent into death about as difficult as it gets because it is noisy with life.

Most of us regard life’s terminal mystery with a mix of fear and curiosity—the end and the beginning. Omega & Alpha. 

I spent a total of sixteen months hospitalized in Rochester’s Mayo St. Marys, until I faced imminent death from sepsis caused by a driveline infection in my abdomen that slowly spread to the tiny titanium pump embedded below my heart.

The infection quickly reached my heart and blood. 

Between the covers

My wife Beth transcribed 340 poems from the Moleskine notebooks I kept for sixty-four months as a Destination Therapy LVAD patient.

[Editor’s note: This ‘left ventricular assist device’ (LVAD) therapy is a treatment for patients with end-stage heart failure who are not candidates for a heart transplant.]

Verbatim clinical notes, inserted into the narrative, describe everything doctors and nurses faced trying to keep me alive as long as possible. 

My musings on dogs and death, pain, love, and longing explore the vagaries of Dying Man’s extraordinary life, his many good deeds and many sins.

“Lest you think the book—“Dying Man Suite”—will be another just-the-facts medical book about how different medicines and a heart transplant saved his life, forget it,” wrote John Weiss in a Root River Current profile. “Driscoll was writing, mostly poetry. Sometimes he would write on a Mayo notepad and tape that into one of his diaries,” Weiss shared. (See samples from Driscoll’s diaries and read more about his life’s journey in On His Own Terms: The Writing Life of Tom Driscoll(opens in new tab).)

A book launch with readings and discussion earlier this summer marked the end of my Minnesota Arts Board-funded writing project. 

Tom Driscoll held his capstone discussion and reading at the Chateau Theatre in Rochester, June 30, 2026. (Submitted photo)

“Dying Man Suite” is the product of Minnesota taxpayers’ generosity, the generosity of an anonymous donor who gave me the gift of life in 2021, and the unselfish effort of easily hundreds of medical professionals in Winona, La Crosse, and at Mayo Clinic in Rochester; and my friends & family—most of all my dear wife Beth Stanford.

The following excerpts reflect the book’s general character and presentation. Described by its publisher as a “literary tour de force,” a hybrid poetry collection & personal memoir annotated with clinical notes, “Dying Man Suite” is available from Shipwreckt Books(opens in new tab).

July 13, 2016 

“Elongated limbs swarmed between EMTs to worm my rigid carcass off the ambulance gurney onto a transport bed, stripping me and rolling me into a robe. Blood flowed backward out of my ruined heart into a dark abyss. Yet a placebo calm submerged me in fetal warmth, knowing I had arrived at “The Mayo,” as my Rushford neighbors called it. 

Capped and masked, a nurse in green scrubs covered me with a white flannel blanket. She took command of my gurney, snapped the siderails into place, jacked that fancy sucker up, kicked off the brake and transferred me from the contemplation of a gray concrete ceiling over the ambulance bay to the relentless, impartial gaze of flowing white rectangles and glowing panel lights hovering over the corridors, deep inside the Saint Mother Marys Mothership to the CCU where I lay helpless across the universe from my worried wife and stunned family members. My body warped in vertigo around the narrow axis of a ventilator pipe.”

“Mr. Driscoll has sustained a large myocardial infarction … The mitral valve looks good. We are preparing to extubate him tonight. Currently, I do not see any indication to consider either ECMO, left ventricular assist device, or other assisted circulatory devices …” 13-Jul-2016: Dr. Joseph G. Murphy MD.

July 14, 2016

“When I wasn’t in a fearless bareknuckle fight for survival, I was confessing all my sins of all time to all who asked. Doctors and fellows delved into the utter hurricane of my past and recent behaviors with leading questions. Now that my life had suddenly stopped cold in the present, entirely disabled, I worried about my traumatized wife Beth, and of course my dogs. Everything planned and pending suddenly ended up in limbo with unbaptized babies and me.”

“I wasn’t ready for the level and intensity of Mayo Clinic’s top-tier providers. Whip smart, like the Gundersen team, professionals who had trained all their lives to find me where I was; but I wasn’t there. I ruminated on the other side of the wonderverse, cleaving my soul as securely as I could against my broken heart while the Mayo astronomers gawped deep inside looking for me.”

“… Regarding events during hospitalization, Mr. Driscoll … specifically mentioned looking at the clock in his room and writing down the time multiple times and recognizing how the time and events will start repeating throughout the day … he mentioned that all the things that occurred … were things he experienced before and he knew everything ahead of time.” 14-Jul-2016: Saint Marys Hospital, Mary Brigh 3C.

October 12, 2016 

(Back home in Rushford, unable to do much of anything but change and charge my batteries and feel sick.) “I had to silently acknowledge the obvious fact that our established spousal roles, Tom & Beth, had reversed and would remain reversed for the rest of my life. I referred to this period of irreversible role reversal as “When I died,” which of course Beth did not like to hear. The upshot was moot, I guess, because after I died, I followed Beth’s lead. Even on our out-of-control house renovation project.

“When I undertook my Five-Year Plan to rehabilitate a structurally decrepit house in the summer of 2000, I counted forty-nine windows in the two-story plus full walkup attic made three—where half of Rushford men under seventy remembered playing basketball when they were growing up. What was I thinking? 

I wanted to write and to be otherwise unemployed while I pondered the sensory imagery of my universe. I still needed a plausible explanation for what the hell we were doing moving to Rushford, a town of fewer than 1,200 souls at the time. Fixing up the wreck up-side the bluff smack under the white masonry Rushford sign hundreds of feet above explained most everything. 

“If someone pressed me to single out the primary cause of my glorious infarction, I would blame every-damn-thing, from the perspective of Dying Man returning home with his heart in a bag—his delicious hallucinations; his serial gambits of preemptive depression; his retreat from matrimonial and familial stability; his pigheaded estrangement from his daughters and his five grandchildren; and his DNA wrought lifelong writing, editing, and publishing addiction, moving at the speed of senescence fading to black—I would blame my blasted, life-altering heart attack on the deep, inescapable fester of dread & guilt & loneliness caused by That Old House on Silk-stocking Avenue, as a short stretch of rotting or removed Gilded-Age-inspired gingerbread houses from the nineteenth century was known in the indomitable little Lutheran town of Rushford, Minnesota.”

Three Short Poems

 

Sunny. 30. Don’t feel well

3/16/2019

Touched too many door knobs this week.

 

Tai Chi

May 8, 2020

The                                push

back

of                                air

hands

 

standing at a 

high point below

the thick buckskin

oil painted on

grasses invaded by

staghorn sumac

my withered arms

one at a time

sweep a great circle

to grasp hands and bow.

Would it be fine

4/5/21

to die today

tomorrow?”

Contributor

Tom Driscoll

Tom Driscoll is a multifaceted writer known for his work in publishing, journalism and the arts. He is Managing Editor & CEO of Winona-based Shipwreckt Books Publishing Co. & Lost Lake Folk Opera magazine. Previously a resident of Rushford, Minn., he now lives in Winona.
